Specification Draft PR #2159 Problem and scope A payment institution needs to distinguish a customer’s business entries from changes to the spending capacity it grants. It also needs to connect individual entries, current-period totals, and sealed periods when reconciling customer funds. An institution-level aggregate does not provide those per-account records. This proposal defines a common contract interface for those records and controls. It can serve an institution’s own business independently or compose with an on-chain payment protocol. It does not issue or transfer assets, establish customer identity, or prove that funds have been frozen or settled. Account model and interface Each account is scoped by (account, institution) . An institution can serve payer accounts, merchant accounts, or both; the same address at two institutions does not share records or capacity. Holding the account’s private key does not grant permission to write entries. Current state contains a limit baseline, cumulative outflows and inflows, and a user-period identifier: available = limit + credit - debit The three amounts and the resulting available capacity must fit in uint96 ; arithmetic uses wider intermediates and rejects negative capacity or out-of-range results. Five write operations separate the relevant responsibilities: addLimit and subLimit adjust the baseline without changing business-entry totals

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.12100v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems increasingly appear in criminal investigations as tools, targets, and sources of evidence, yet AI forensics lacks a systematic account of the artifacts they produce: investigators often do not know which traces to look for, and for many traces they do find, no established analysis technique exists. In this paper we first developed the Forensic AI Life Cycle (FALC) that unlike other life cycle models shifts the focus onto the forensic artifacts created during the life cycle of an AI system. Through FALC we derived a reference list of artifacts that might serve an investigation. Second, we collected examples for crimes with AI involvement throughout FALC and questions likely to be asked when investigating these crimes. Third, we propose a taxonomy of forensic fields of expertise with a focus on the current possibility to analyze AI forensic artifacts using established techniques. For investigators, the model provides a systematic basis for identifying which artifacts to look for when an AI system is relevant to a case. For researchers, the classification shows where existing forensic methods already suffice and where new techniques are most urgently needed.
events.title: FALC: An Artifact-Centric Life Cycle Model and Research Agenda for AI Forensics

events.excerpt: arXiv:2606.24389v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Interactive virtual reality (VR) streaming over Wi-Fi requires stringent latency and reliability guarantees, which become increasingly difficult to achieve under dynamic channel conditions and shared-medium contention. These challenges make real-time bitrate adaptation a critical yet fundamentally difficult control problem, particularly under limited visibility of network conditions. This paper formulates VR bitrate adaptation as a network-aware, online decision-making problem and proposes BRAVR, a decentralized deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithm that combines application-layer observations with lightweight wireless statistics collected at the Wi-Fi access point (AP) to balance visual quality, streaming performance, and multi-user airtime fairness. We implement BRAVR in a real VR streaming system and evaluate it on a physical Wi-Fi testbed against the VR-tailored NeSt-VR algorithm and an ablated BRAVR variant without AP telemetry. Experimental results show that, in the evaluated scenarios, BRAVR consistently achieves its design objectives, delivering robust quality of service (QoS) while avoiding sustained airtime overutilization. It also outperforms the AP-blind ablation, demonstrating the value of incorporating network-level information into the bitrate adaptation control loop. Overall, these results demonstrate the potential of AP-assisted online learning for decentralized interactive VR streaming over commodity Wi-Fi and provide practical insights into bitrate adaptation in shared wireless environments.
events.title: BRAVR: An AP-Assisted Online DRL Mechanism for Interactive VR Bitrate Adaptation over Wi-Fi

events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.11754v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate advantage distillation for paired-state Loop-Back quantum key distribution, with a fixed optical station serving a lightweight portable terminal. Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses, Bob selects and applies a polarization filter to each pulse, and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The proposed advantage-distillation step selects consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph. The closing edge of a parity polygon is shown to be redundant: any spanning tree of the same vertices has the same acceptance set. We derive exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates. Under independent bit errors, the three-record filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, while its cost in discarded records and public information is accounted for explicitly. A modular security theorem bounds the additional guessing advantage available to an adversary after syndrome disclosure and block acceptance, including arbitrary quantum side information. We also evaluate a specified single-photon passive-tap optical channel, obtaining a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities. This parity-based advantage-distillation step detects discrepancies by postselection; it does not correct individual errors and is intended to precede conventional reconciliation. events.excerpt: arXiv:2611.10595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The limited computational resources of Internet of Things (IoT) devices present challenges for secure image processing. This paper presents a distributed chaotic image encryption system using independent Wi-Fi-connected ESP32-S3 microcontrollers. A master-worker architecture distributes image blocks through master-coordinated chaotic sequence management, maintaining one logically continuous chaotic sequence by assigning block-specific starting states independently of worker assignments. The implemented system uses reversible chaotic substitution (SUBSTITUTE), while Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)-signed discovery messages and Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 with mutual authentication secure device communication. Experimental evaluation using one, two, and four workers demonstrates a reduction in execution time from 43.215 to 15.878 seconds, achieving a speed-up of 2.72 times. The encrypted image achieves a Shannon entropy of 7.999940 bits/byte and near-zero adjacent-pixel correlation. Exact image recovery is verified through matching Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) hashes and a Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) value of 1.0. Additional experiments demonstrate successful encryption and decryption using different worker counts and block sizes, automatic task reassignment following worker failure, and rejection of a mismatched private key during TLS authentication. events.excerpt: arXiv:2208.03784v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: There is growing awareness that the analysis of personal data, such as individuals' mobility, financial, and health data, can provide significant benefits to society. However, liberal societies have so far refrained from such analytics, arguably due to the lack of secure analytics platforms that scale to billions of records while operating in a very strong threat model. We contend that one fundamental gap here is the lack of an architecture that can scale (actively-)secure multi-party computation (MPC) horizontally without weakening security. To bridge this gap, we present CoVault, an analytics platform that leverages server-aided MPC and trusted execution environments (TEEs) to colocate the MPC parties in a single datacenter without reducing security, and scales MPC horizontally to the datacenter's available resources. CoVault scales well empirically. For example, CoVault can scale the DualEx 2PC protocol to perform epidemic analytics for a country of 80M people (about 11.85B data records/day) on a continuous basis using one core pair for every 30,000 people.
events.title: CoVault: Secure, Scalable Analytics of Personal Data

An agent keeps its identity while its code, dependencies, memories, skills, plans and ways of judging keep changing. events.excerpt: Description Clean builds of sui-node are slow: about 164s in dev and about 296s in release on a 16-core Mac. This cuts them to about 130s in dev and about 231s in release without removing functionality. Each commit stands alone: Drop unneeded crates from the graph. sui-simulator re-exported Move package and build crates that nothing used. These pulled move-compiler and sui-sdk into the build. sui-indexer-alt-metrics now puts its postgres collector behind a postgres feature, so diesel and postgres are no longer built. No host build of sui-types for a build script. sui-package-management 's build.rs now reads the snapshot manifest JSON directly instead of depending on sui-framework-snapshot . Less code generation in sui-core . Spawn helpers box futures before tokio::spawn , so tokio compiles one task harness instead of one per future type. This costs one extra allocation per spawn. typed-store 's DBMap / SafeIter methods move the code that doesn't depend on the key and value types into non-generic functions. SuiNode::start_async returns a boxed future, so node startup compiles once in the sui-node library instead of again in the binary. rocksdb no longer waits for jemalloc. rocksdb's jemalloc feature only enables jemalloc's unprefixed malloc. The C++ define it adds isn't read by rocksdb's sources. typed-store now turns on that jemalloc feature directly, so rocksdb's C++ build script starts without waiting for jemalloc's. The resolved jemalloc features are the same as before. Test plan Covered by existing tests for the changed crates. Timings come from alternating clean cargo

It is otherwise identical to op-deployer/v0.9.0 . Other changes Deploy To deploy or upgrade a chain with op-contracts/v9.0.0+allowlist, set opcmAddress in the intent to the allowlist OPCM. That address is 0x12f00d96414fe43cc3a19acc1254d7bd83d5bed0 on Mainnet and 0xb72366fb8f855779f01800aed1ebfae886f37ace on Sepolia. This requires intent type custom or standard-overrides , because a standard intent rejects any OPCM other than the registry's. Without opcmAddress , op-deployer uses the op-contracts/v9.0.0 OPCM from the superchain registry, as v0.9.0 does ( #23929 , #23933 ) Full Changelog : op-deployer/v0.9.0...op-deployer/v0.9.0-allowlist 🚢 Docker Image: https://us-docker.pkg.dev/oplabs-tools-artifacts/images/op-deployer:v0.9.0-allowlist

events.excerpt: Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running. Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post , we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage. We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. events.excerpt: Abstract This standard defines a proxy that coordinates execution sessions by temporarily caching a program and its associated calldata in transient storage. The proxy forwards the cached program to a fixed implementation through DELEGATECALL and uses a handler flag to control whether subsequent reentrant invocations are dispatched. The program remains unchanged throughout an execution session, while the cached calldata is replaced on each accepted invocation. This enables a single implementation to coordinate callback-driven execution using different programs and calldata without deploying a new contract for each execution. Motivation Many advanced execution strategies require dynamically changing execution logic, particularly when interacting with external contracts that invoke callbacks during execution. Traditionally, dynamically changing the execution logic of a contract may require deploying a new contract containing the desired runtime code. This introduces deployment costs, including contract creation and code-deposit costs. Flash Loan Proxy separates the execution program from the implementation responsible for interpreting it. events.excerpt: Executive summary Ethereum’s upcoming enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS) introduces new ways for validators to participate in block-building markets. Most importantly, it enables builders to compete directly for block proposals, with payments guaranteed by the Ethereum protocol, reducing the need for trusted intermediaries. This proposal seeks to preserve the principles of Lido’s existing MEV Policy while adapting it to ePBS: maximizing rewards for stakers, supporting open and competitive block-building markets, and ensuring that Node Operators (NOs) do not favor particular builders or withhold MEV rewards. Following the discussion in Lido’s call for an updated MEV policy . It proposes a two-track approach: 1. An open, permissionless market where Lido validators can accept bids from any builder meeting Ethereum’s protocol requirements, provided payments are guaranteed by the protocol. 2. A vetted market where builders and intermediaries offering additional payments outside Ethereum’s guarantees must be approved through Lido’s Allowed List. Both tracks apply regardless of how a bid arrives: via p2p, a direct connection, or through one of the available sidecars. APR is maximized as operators can source from the full market; MEV hiding remains detectable because every bid is signed and attributable; and the trust previously placed in relays (now builders) is either removed or explicitly scoped through regular governance. events.excerpt: Discussion topic for EIP-8477: Recent Block Bound Delegation Authorizations . Motivated by the recent EIP-7702 sweeps that happened on Binance 16 this proposal in essence prevents long term storage of EIP-7702 signatures for later playback. This proposal limits the delayed use of unused EIP-7702 authorizations. Each authorization signs a recent execution block number and its block header hash, in addition to the existing chain ID, delegation address, and nonce. For inclusion in execution block N , the signed block must be one of its preceding 256 ancestors and its hash must match that ancestor. An anchor exactly 256 blocks behind remains eligible; one 257 blocks behind is ineligible. The current block and future blocks are excluded. Freshness is checked during native authorization processing, before signature recovery or authority-specific state access. An expired or mismatched anchor skips that authorization using EIP-7702’s existing skip-on-failure behavior. It does not consume the authority’s nonce through that entry or clear an existing delegation. Structurally malformed authorizations invalidate the transaction. The draft applies the same freshness requirement to installation, replacement, and zero-address revocation. Installed delegations remain in effect after their authorization’s anchor expires. The proposal limits the inclusion window of an unused signature; it does not expire installed delegation or prevent an attacker with live signing access from promptly using a fresh signature.
